chronicle/the-book-of-broken-roads.body:
> Whether the builders of the Witness Roads spoke to the dead or merely recorded them, I cannot tell you — and I was there.

I am Ilthen Vael, once Third Recorder of the waystation at Grey Weir, struck from the rolls of the Order of Witnesses in the year 2231 of the Road Reckoning for the crime of refusing to die. The ragged folk of the hearthlands call me **Ledgerbone**, and leave tallow candles at my door in winter, which is kind and useless. I do not eat. I do not sleep. I write.

I took the Second Interment — the rite the living call *lichdom*, spitting sideways as they say it — for one reason, and I set it here at the front of the book so no reader mistakes me: **records die with their recorders.** Parchment rots. Stone shears. Memory flatters. A witness who cannot die is the only archive that keeps itself. I chose to become a dead thing that remembers, and I have never once regretted it, and the price I paid is written in [V. The Recorder's Bargain](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/v-the-recorder-s-bargain) where it belongs, as an entry like any other.

> **The chronicler's vow.** This book records events, not motives. Where I saw a thing, I say so. Where I copied a seal, I name the seal. Where accounts conflict, I give the conflict and do not resolve it. A history that claims to know why men did what they did is not a history; it is a eulogy, or an indictment. The Witnessry taught me that much before it cast me out, and it is the one oath of theirs I never broke.

What follows is the history of the world of **Theandril** from the unwritten dark to the present hour — the hour in which new banners rise over the rekindled hearths, and maps and promises have become valuable again. It ends where your own record must begin.

---

## The order of the book

1. [I. The Unwritten World](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/i-the-unwritten-world) — what came before records, and why I will not invent it.
2. [II. The Age of First Oaths](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/ii-the-age-of-first-oaths) — the hearth peoples, the fourteen springs of magic, and the First Sealing at Cold Ford.
3. [III. The Raising of the Roads](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/iii-the-raising-of-the-roads) — how the Witness Roads were built, what they did, and what they cost.
4. [IV. The Age of Crowns](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/iv-the-age-of-crowns) — the five great powers of the old world, and the rot that ripened under the gold.
5. [V. The Recorder's Bargain](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/v-the-recorder-s-bargain) — my mortal life, my death, and the terms of my continuing.
6. [VI. The Reckoning](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/vi-the-reckoning) — the wars that broke the world: the War of Written Fire, the Severing, the Hollowing.
7. [VII. The Failing and the Ashfall](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/vii-the-failing-and-the-ashfall) — the two years in which the Roads went quiet and the sky came down.
8. [VIII. The Long Ash](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/viii-the-long-ash) — one hundred and thirty-four years of ruin, and what crawled out of it.
9. [IX. The Rekindled Hearths](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/ix-the-rekindled-hearths) — the four powers of the present hour: Compact, Council, March, and Tide.
10. [X. The Present Hour](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/x-the-present-hour) — the world as it stands in RR 2447, at the dawn of a new Age of Fracture.
11. [Appendix — The Fourteen Traditions](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/appendix-the-fourteen-traditions) — the springs of magic and the nine disciplines, for readers who will need them.

---

*On reckoning: I count years from the First Sealing at Cold Ford — the Road Reckoning, written RR. The Roads stood for two thousand three hundred and eleven years. They have been quiet for one hundred and thirty-six. The living have begun counting again from their own little foundings, each hearthland with its own calendar, which is how you know an age has truly broken.*

chronicle/i-the-unwritten-world.body:
> Before the first stone was sealed, the world already owed itself a debt. — carving above the drowned door at Cold Ford, author unknown

Every people in Theandril keeps a story of the beginning, and every story contradicts the others, and I have outlived enough theologians to say plainly: **no account of the world's making is attested by any witness.** I record the three tellings that held the widest allegiance in the old world, and I rank them by the number of their believers, not by their truth, which is not mine to weigh.

## The three tellings

- **The Kiln.** The mountain peoples — the deep-folk of the Anvilheights foremost — hold that the world was fired like a vessel in a kiln, and came out flawed, and that the flaw runs through everything: every vein of ore, every heart. Work, in this telling, is worship: to forge, to mend, to shore up the crack. The Iron Covenant built two thousand years of doctrine on it.
- **The First Bargain.** The hearth peoples of the river plains taught that the world began as an agreement between the land and the dead — the living permitted to plant and build in exchange for remembrance. Break the remembering, and the lease fails. After the Ashfall, you will understand, this telling acquired a terrible new congregation.
- **The Drowned Star.** Along the coasts they said a star fell burning into the first sea, and everything that lives crawled out of the scald. The fen courts kept a crueler version: that the star is still down there, still burning, and the tides are its breathing. Sailors of the Saltwind League swore by it. Their descendants on the Glass Coast have particular reasons, now, to remember it.

---

## What can be attested

The oldest things in Theandril that a sober witness can touch are these: the **waystones before the Roads** — raw standing stones on hilltops and fords, older than any nation, already ancient when the Witnessry claimed them; the **bone terraces** of the southern chalklands, burial architecture on a scale no living people could explain, which the Sepulchral Synod would later inherit and put to use; and the **fourteen springs of magic**, which are not places but inheritances — the traditions of Flame and Storm, Tide and Stone, Verdancy and Grave, Star and Dream, Shadow and Radiance, Spirit and Rune, Oath, and the one we do not name in charity, the Void. No one taught the first peoples these arts. They were found in the blood and the land the way a river is found: already running. Their natures are set out in the [Appendix — The Fourteen Traditions](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/appendix-the-fourteen-traditions).

Of the elder ancestries I will say only what I have seen or copied. The deep-folk of the mountains are attested in every age, patient and closed. The fen-courts of the Deepfen are older than their own records and pleased to keep it so. Giants are attested in three reliable accounts and several hundred unreliable ones. The dead are attested everywhere, always, in every ledger of the world; whatever else changes, the dead accumulate. And there were things in the far places — the high cold, the deep dark, the wide water — that never sent an envoy or signed a bargain, and hold their domains to this hour.

> A marginal note, in my own later hand: I have been asked, by kings and by children, what *I* believe of the beginning. I believe the world is old, and owed, and that nobody alive holds the note. Beyond that I decline to testify.

chronicle/ii-the-age-of-first-oaths.body:
> Say it at the stone, or do not say it at all. — hearth proverb, older than the Roads

Before roads there were fords, and before nations there were hearths. The first order of the world was small and fierce: a longhouse, a well, a wall, a fire that must not go out. What the hearth peoples lacked in numbers they made up in *memory* — and memory, in Theandril, was never a private thing. It was spoken aloud, at stones, before witnesses. This chapter records how that habit became the bones of civilization.

## The oath culture

A bargain spoken at a waystone was held to bind in a way no whispered promise could. Whether the stones themselves listened was already disputed then — I ask the reader to grow accustomed to that sentence, for it recurs through this entire book like a debt that is never paid down. What is attested is the *practice*: grain-shares, marriages, borders, blood-prices, all sworn at the stones before the assembled dead of both parties, whose names were recited so they might attend. Oathbreaking was rare and its punishment was not death but **erasure** — the breaker's name struck from every recitation, so that no ancestor would know him and no stone would hold his word again. Men who would cheerfully hang preferred not to be erased.

From the oath culture rose the first arts of rule: tally-sticks, then marks, then true writing, which the hearth peoples always regarded as a lesser, portable form of the stone-spoken word. The Oath tradition of magic — bindings, lineage-rites, the coercive sanctities that would one day be so catastrophically abused — grew up alongside, tangled with the Spirit tradition's ancestor-craft and the Grave tradition's quiet offices. Magic in this age was parochial, hedge-taught, and held in awe. There were no colleges. There was the woman at the edge of the marsh, and you went to her politely.

---

## The Witnessry

In the year now reckoned RR 1, at the ford called Cold Ford on the river Sallow, the elders of nineteen hearth communities did a new thing: they sealed a stone **jointly**, binding not one bargain but a standing service — that the stone at Cold Ford would hold *any* lawful bargain brought before it, for any party, in exchange for a toll of grain and remembrance. They appointed keepers to sit the stone in rotation, take testimony, and cut the seals. These keepers were the first of the **Order of Witnesses**, my order, and the toll-station they built beside the ford was the first waystation.

The invention spread the way fire spreads in a dry year, because it answered the oldest problem of the scattered hearths: *how do you trust a stranger?* You do not. You trust the stone between you. Within three generations there were forty waystations; within ten, four hundred, each sealed to its neighbors so that a bargain cut at one could be attested at all. The paths between them wore deep with feet and hooves and were paved by subscription, and men began to call the whole — stones, stations, keepers, paths, and the invisible lattice of held bargains — by a single name: **the Witness Roads.**

> What the keepers actually did at the stones, I will describe in [III. The Raising of the Roads](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/iii-the-raising-of-the-roads) — from practice, not hearsay, for it was my work for twenty-one years. What I will not describe is what the stones did. Not because it was secret. Because I do not know.

chronicle/iii-the-raising-of-the-roads.body:
> The Roads did not carry goods. Goods went by cart. The Roads carried the reason men dared load the cart.

It is already hard, one long lifetime after the Failing, to make the young understand what the Witness Roads *were*. They hear 'roads' and think of paving. Let me be exact, as an old clerk is entitled to be.

## What the Roads were

A waystation was a tolled crossing — a ford, a pass, a harbor mouth — with a sealed waystone at its heart and a chapter of Witnesses in residence. A traveler paid the toll in grain, coin, or recitation. A party to a bargain paid more, and got more: testimony taken under rite, the bargain cut into wax and lead, the seal registered at the stone, and — this was the whole of it — **the bargain attested at every other stone on the network.** A grain factor in the Anvilheights could strike terms with a fleet owner of the Outer Isles, neither having met the other, each trusting not the man but the lattice. Credit crossed mountains. Brides and hostages and treaties crossed. Peace, of a working kind, crossed.

The mechanism of attestation is the great disputed matter of all Theandril's history, and I give the dispute honestly. The doctrine of my own order held that the stones **recorded**: that a seal cut under rite was impressed into the lattice as a mark is pressed into wax, mindless and exact. The folk conviction, never once dislodged by doctrine, held that the stones **listened**: that the recited dead attended the stones, and that it was the dead who carried word from ford to ford, tireless couriers in the dark, and that this was why bargains were spoken *to* the stone with the ancestors' names called first. I sat a stone for twenty-one years. I took ten thousand testimonies. I felt — I will permit myself this single unclerkly sentence in the whole of this book — I felt *attended*. Make of it what you will. Both doctrines fit every fact I possess, including the facts of the Failing.

---

## What the Roads made possible

- **Distance without treachery.** The hearthlands knitted into one commercial world. The great fairs rose at the junction stations; the junction stations became towns; the towns, cities.
- **Credit.** A sealed bargain could be pledged against another. This began honestly, as seed-corn loans. Hold the thought, for it is the worm in the apple, and it eats through [IV. The Age of Crowns](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/iv-the-age-of-crowns) to the end.
- **Law.** Erasure became excommunication from commerce itself. To be struck from the stones was civil death, and the fear of it governed better than any army.
- **The Witnessry's estate.** Four hundred stations' tolls made my order rich, and richer than rich: *necessary*. We swore neutrality to every crown and were mostly believed, and mostly deserved it, for longer than most orders keep any oath at all.

The raising ran eight centuries, and I mark the Age of First Oaths as ending when the last blank space on the network closed — when a bargain could travel from the far Anvilheights to the southern chalk without leaving attested ground. After that, the world the Roads had made began to make powers worthy of it. Their story is [IV. The Age of Crowns](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/iv-the-age-of-crowns). The price of it all is [VI. The Reckoning](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/vi-the-reckoning).

> Toll ledgers from Grey Weir, years RR 2210–2231, survive in my keeping, copied in my own mortal hand. Whatever else in this book is doubted, those numbers are exact, and I will show them to any honest scholar who is not afraid of my house.

chronicle/iv-the-age-of-crowns.body:
> Gold is a promise that has forgotten who made it. — attributed to the Widow of the Deepfen; the attribution is not attested

For fifteen centuries — call it RR 800 to the eve of the Reckoning — the world was large, loud, and ruled. Five great powers dominated the attested lands, with a hundred lesser crowns, free cities, monster domains, mercenary hosts, and cult enclaves in the seams between them. I served the Roads through the last golden century of this age and its whole rotten aftermath, and I knew the great powers as a clerk knows his richest clients: by their seals, their debts, and their lies.

## The five powers

### The Iron Covenant

The deep-folk holds of the Anvilheights and their human client valleys, bound by the Kiln faith into one disciplined estate. Peerless in metallurgy, masonry, and the Rune and Stone traditions; their artificers' sealed work — self-turning locks, ever-burning forges, the great null-anchors of later infamy — commanded any price. Weak in Dream and Verdancy, and proud of the weakness: *a folk that does not dream does not lie to itself.* They said that. They believed it. Remember it when you reach the Reckoning.

### The Saltwind League

The charter fleets of the Outer Isles and the long coasts — not a kingdom but a lattice of shipping compacts, as the Roads were a lattice of stones. Masters of Tide, Storm, and Star craft, of navigation and of *paper*: the League invented the pledged cargo, the insured keel, the oath-debt sold to a third party. By the late age a League charter was itself a currency, and the High Charter of the Anchorage was crowned in everything but name. Their last High Charter, **Aldery, fourth of that name, the Debt-Crowned**, mortgaged three generations of unborn oaths to fund a trade war, and the stones held the pledge, because the stones held everything. The reader sees where this book is going.

### The Mire Courts

The elder courts of the great southern wetland, the Deepfen — fen-folk older than their own records, governing by season, ceremony, and patience. Deep in Verdancy, Spirit, and Dream; disdainful of heavy works; unconquerable at home, indifferent abroad. The Courts joined the Roads late, used them sparingly, and withdrew from them — I record the fact, and the year, RR 2289, and note that of all the powers of the old world, only the Mire Courts withdrew *before* the catastrophe. The folk of the Reedfen margin, who would one day be the Reedbound Council, were their tenants, tributaries, and unacknowledged children.

### The Sepulchral Synod

The priest-state of the southern chalklands, inheritors of the bone terraces, where the dead of forty generations were housed, ranked, and — their word — *employed*. Grave, Star, and Shadow were their estates; necromantic logistics their unmatched art. Synod caravans crossed deserts without water, Synod terraces raised harvests with tireless labor, and no plague, famine, or war ever produced in Synod lands the mass graves it produced elsewhere, because in Synod lands a grave was a beginning, not an end. Other realms traded with them eagerly and washed afterward. The Synod's hierarch, the **Provost of the Ninth Terrace**, was never in my long lifetime named, seen unveiled, or attested dead. It was the Synod that granted my petition, and I owe them my continuing, and I mark my debt here where every reader can see it and weigh my testimony accordingly.

### The Null Throne

The human kingdom of the Middle Reach — the old heart of the hearthlands, ruling from **Wardhall** over the river plains where Cold Ford itself stood. The Throne's founding grievance was magic itself: a dynasty raised on the wreckage of a sorcerers' war, sworn to the doctrine that the fourteen springs were fourteen leaks in the hull of the world. Modest in spellcraft by law; formidable beyond measure in Warding, engineering, and the arts of *nullification* — mage-hunters, ward-lines, and, in the last century, Covenant-forged null-anchors that could silence a working across a whole valley. The Throne guarded the greatest density of waystations in the world and took its tolls gravely. When the reader learns, in [VI. The Reckoning](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/vi-the-reckoning), who first cut a waystation dead on purpose, the reader will already have guessed.

---

## The rot under the gold

The crowned age died of its own bookkeeping, and I watched the entries accumulate. Set these four side by side, in the order the stones met them:

1. **Oath-debt.** Bargains pledged against bargains, pledges sold, the sold pledges pledged again. By RR 2250 the lattice held perhaps forty times more promised value than the world contained. No one intended this. Everyone profited by it. The Witnessry registered it all, neutrally, as was our oath, and our neutrality was the load-bearing wall of the whole tower.
2. **Soul collateral.** It began in the Synod's lawful practice — labor of the housed dead, pledged like any other yield — and spread as fashion among the desperate and the vile everywhere: remembrance itself put up as security. A man's recitation, his standing with his own dead, forfeit on default. The Oath and Grave traditions twisted together into instruments the first hearth peoples would have burned us all for. The stones held these pledges too. They held anything lawfully sworn. That was the whole of their virtue, and the whole of the horror.
3. **Counterfeit seals.** In RR 2263 a Veilcraft working surfaced in the Anchorage that could dress a false bargain in a true seal. It was suppressed, its makers hanged in their own rigging at the Anchorage Feast — the League fed its guests first; they were civilized — and it surfaced again, and again, for it was too useful to die. Every forged seal that passed attested was a coal laid against the day the whole ledger would be asked to prove itself.
4. **The mortgaging of the Witnessry.** Last and worst, and I record it against my own order. Stations took standing pensions from crowns. Chapters ruled on disputes their patrons had interests in. We remained honest in the small and were purchased in the large, and we told ourselves the lattice was sound because the *stones* were sound. First Recorder **Maude of Grey Weir**, my teacher, was hanged in RR 2229 by a League factor's court for refusing to backdate a seal. The order's protest was filed, registered, and attested at four hundred stones. No one was punished. That was the Age of Crowns, entire, in one entry.

> I have been accused of writing this chapter coldly. I sat the stone at Grey Weir while the age described here mortgaged the world. Cold is what I have instead of screaming.

chronicle/v-the-recorder-s-bargain.body:
> You are asking to be the last man at every deathbed. — the Provost's examiner, at my petition; the one sentence of the interview I was permitted to keep

Here I set down my own entry, at its place in the sequence, no longer and no more tender than the age deserves. A history from the mouth of a lich owes the reader an accounting of the mouth.

## The mortal ledger

Born RR 2183 in the toll-town under Grey Weir, on the river Sallow, third child of a weigh-clerk. The ash-lung took my brothers in the outbreak of 2191; it spared me with nothing worse than the wheeze I carried until I no longer needed breath. Apprenticed to the station at fourteen — a boy who could cut a straight seal was fed, and my father knew it. Sworn Witness at twenty. Third Recorder at twenty-seven, under First Recorder Maude, who taught me the whole of my craft and most of my conscience. I married a boatwright's daughter, Senna, in RR 2212. I record her name because she deserves a stone somewhere, and I am the only stone that held.

In RR 2229 Maude was hanged, as set down in [IV. The Age of Crowns](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/iv-the-age-of-crowns), for refusing to falsify the record. I stood in the crowd with the station's ledgers strapped to my back — her last instruction — and I understood two things before her feet stopped. First: the order would not protect the record. Second: the record would die anyway, hanged or honored, because records are kept in meat, and meat fails. Every archive in the world was one fire, one flood, one dishonest generation from silence. The thought did not leave me. Thoughts like that do not leave; they nest.

## The Second Interment

I petitioned the Ninth Terrace in RR 2230. I will not describe the year of examination except to say the Synod refuses more petitions than it grants and is right to, and that they asked me one question in a hundred forms: *what do you wish to keep?* Men who answer 'my life' are refused. Men who answer 'my power' are refused and watched. I answered 'the ledger,' every time, in every form, because it was true, and in the spring of RR 2231 I was granted the rite the terraces call the Second Interment.

Of the rite itself: they bury you alive with your own testament, and what has truly finished with living climbs back out with it. The body dies honestly — I insist on this point against every fireside version — the heart stops, the blood settles, the rot begins and is *arrested*, bound and inked and sealed in place by Grave-craft and Rune-craft and a Forbidden art whose name I hold under oath. What returns is not the man preserved but the man **notarized**: a fair copy of the soul, cut into its own bone. It hurt more than the ash-lung and less than the hanging I watched. I climbed out on the third day with my testament in my teeth, and I have not slept since, and the dark of the grave has never entirely finished being my weather.

## What it cost

- Taste, temperature, sleep, and the wheeze. I miss the wheeze. It was my brothers'.
- My orders. The Witnessry struck me from the rolls within the season — *a Witness must be capable of erasure*, ran the judgment, *and this man has made himself unerasable.* I have had a century to appreciate that they were right by their own law, and I keep their law better than they kept it, so I bear the expulsion lightly.
- Senna. She lived to seventy-one and would not see me after the rite, and she was right too. I did not attend her burial in RR 2266. I recorded it. If the reader wants a definition of what I am, it is there.
- Standing with the living. To the hearthfolk I am Ledgerbone, a horror that files. They are not wrong. A lich is a Forbidden thing, and the tradition that made me has drowned villages in its time; I do not petition for the rehabilitation of my kind. I petition for the record, only ever for the record.

> Why the Synod grants such rites at all, I do not know and do not guess; this book does not deal in motives, mine excepted, and mine are on the table. I was made to remember. Everything after the spring of RR 2231 in this book, I witnessed with these eyes or copied from a named source. Weigh me accordingly.

chronicle/vi-the-reckoning.body:
> The last age of the old world spent twenty years proving that everything the stones held could be spent as a weapon, and the stones held everything.

Historians who came before me liked clean beginnings for wars. I am a clerk; I give the reader entries, in order, and the shape assembles itself. The Reckoning ran, by my accounting, from RR 2291 to the Failing in 2311 — twenty years in which the powers of [IV. The Age of Crowns](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/iv-the-age-of-crowns) turned the machinery of trust into ordnance and fired it at one another until the machinery itself gave way.

## The War of Written Fire — RR 2291–2298

It began as a paper war. A cache of counterfeit seals — true-dressed, decades deep — was uncovered in the Anchorage in RR 2291, implicating League houses, Throne customs officers, and, catastrophically, two chapters of the Witnessry. Every power in the world held pledges that might now be false; every power moved at once to enforce, redeem, or repudiate. The stones' lattice, asked simultaneously to prove forty times the world's worth of promises, answered with the sublime indifference of stone: every *lawfully sworn* bargain stood, forged provenance and all. The phrase 'written fire' is from a League pamphlet of 2293: *they have set fire to us in writing.* Armies marched on ledger entries. The Debt-Crowned called in three generations of mortgaged oaths and drowned half the coast's houses in a season. Erasure — the old, holy punishment — was handed out wholesale by partisan chapters, and for the first time in two thousand years men learned to *prefer* erasure, to seek it, because a man struck from the stones owed nothing. Within five years the world contained, for the first time, a class of soldiers with no attested existence. They fought accordingly.

## The Severing — RR 2298–2309

In RR 2298, Warden-King **Ossric, third of the name**, of the Null Throne, did the thing no crown in twenty-three centuries had done: he ordered a waystation killed. Covenant-forged null-anchors were set at the four corners of the station at Reed Ford, and the stone was silenced — not broken, *silenced*, cut from the lattice like a name from a recitation. Every bargain routed through Reed Ford lost attestation in an hour. The Throne's declaration named it surgery: the cutting of corrupted credit from the body of the world. I copied that declaration with these hands, and I copy here what the toll ledgers show instead: every station Ossric severed, in eleven years of surgery, stood on a route that fed his enemies' credit, and none on his own.

The precedent, once set, ran like ash-lung through a toll-town. The League severed stations to void its called debts. Covenant holds severed their own passes to seal the mountains. Free cities severed stations rather than see them enforced against them. Each severed stone dumped its held bargains into dispute, and each dispute fed the armies. By RR 2309, of the four hundred stations of the network's height, perhaps two hundred and sixty still spoke. The lattice held — the Roads' builders had built past all praise — but it held as a wounded man holds: by routing everything through what remained.

## The Hollowing — RR 2305–2311

Last, and worst, and I set it down flatly because there is no way to set it down otherwise. In the starving middle of the war, powers began to draw on the one collateral the stones had held for centuries and no one had dared call: **the pledged dead.** The Synod called in soul-collateral on defaulted bargains at scale — lawfully, I am bound to record, by the letter of instruments freely sworn in greeder generations — and marched the yield. Others, with none of the Synod's law and less of its craft, simply *harvested*: battlefield rites of the Forbidden traditions, whole necropolises drafted, the recited ancestors of erased men taken as salvage on the argument that no attested kin remained to object. Whether the stones' own attending dead — if the stones had attending dead; the reader knows my discipline by now — were drawn upon, conscripted, or consumed, I cannot attest. I record only this correlation, and I have checked it across every surviving ledger in my keeping: from RR 2305, stations began to fail *that no anchor had touched* — going first faint, the seals attesting slower, the recitations echoing thinner, and then quiet. The folk word for those six years is the Hollowing. The folk word is better than any doctrine I have.

> Casualty rolls for the Reckoning do not exist, and I will not invent them. I can attest what I counted from the Grey Weir tower in the war's last autumn: the Sallow ran with pyre-ash for nineteen days, and the toll-road walked with refugees from first light to last, and my station's stone had gone so faint that their bargains — for they still stopped, even then, even starving, to swear their little bargains — could no longer be attested past the next ford. I sealed them anyway. Some things one seals anyway.

chronicle/vii-the-failing-and-the-ashfal.body:
> On the morning of the last day of RR 2311, forty thousand bargains stood attested across the world. By midwinter the number was none.

Two years broke the world: 2311 and 2313. I witnessed both from the tower at Grey Weir, which I had held alone since the chapter fled, and I ask the reader's patience if this chapter's entries are shorter than the age deserves. They were short years. They simply had no bottom.

## The Quiet — RR 2311

The Failing was not an event but a cascade, and its first hours have a hundred claimed causes; I give the three with named sources and let them stand in their contradiction, as my vow requires. A Covenant survivor-roll blames the Throne: a final massed anchor-working meant to silence the Synod's terraces at a stroke. A Synod instrument — I hold a certified copy — blames the harvesters: the lattice's *attending strength*, drawn past some floor no one had ever sounded. A League pilot's log, the humblest and to my eye the most honest, records only that the Anchorage stone went quiet at dawn, mid-attestation, 'like a man dying between one word of the sentence and the next.'

What is attested past dispute is the sequence: the great junction stones went first, and every stone that had routed its speech through them found itself alone within days. Stations did not shatter or burn. They went *quiet* — the seals still cut, the wax still cooled, and nothing answered from anywhere. Within a season, the entire architecture of distant trust in Theandril had ceased to exist. Every bargain became local. Every stranger became a stranger again. Credit — forty times the world's worth of it — did not unwind; it simply vanished, and every granary, army, marriage, treaty, and debt that had stood on it stood, for one long teetering moment, on nothing.

## The collapse of the powers

- **The Saltwind League** died of arithmetic in a winter. Fleets whose keels were pledged paper simply changed masters at sword-point, harbor by harbor. The Anchorage burned in the spring riots. Aldery the Debt-Crowned was put over the side of his own flagship by his creditors, wearing, the pilot's log records, his full chain of office. It does not record whether the chain was weighed first. It would have been like them to weigh it.
- **The Null Throne** held longest, as ward-lines and granaries will, and fell to its own doctrine: with the stones quiet, Wardhall's word could not out-travel rumor, and a throne built on distrust of unseen powers was poorly placed when it became, to every distant province, an unseen power. The Middle Reach shattered into warlord marches within a decade. Ossric's line ended obscurely, which the reader may find either fitting or unbearable; I find it both.
- **The Iron Covenant** sealed the passes — their oldest reflex — and the record with them. What has come out of the Anvilheights since the Failing is trade-goods, closed faces, and no answers. I do not attest the Covenant fell. I attest that the mountains closed, and hold.
- **The Mire Courts** had withdrawn in RR 2289, and the Deepfen endured the Failing as wetlands endure most things: by already being poor in promises and rich in mud. Their tenants on the Reedfen margin fared worse, and remembered who had not warned them; that memory is a living politics, and its heirs appear in [IX. The Rekindled Hearths](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/ix-the-rekindled-hearths).
- **The Sepulchral Synod** endures, terraces and Provost and silence entire. The chalklands admit no census-takers. I say of my patrons only what the roads say: the caravans still cross the dry country, still need no water, and pay their tolls now in seed-grain, which the hungry margins accept and do not question aloud.

## The Ashfall — RR 2313

Two years into the Quiet, with the wars guttering for want of anything left to pledge, came the catastrophe the living remember when they say *the world ended* — for the Quiet beggared the world, but the Ashfall burned it. In high summer of RR 2313, fire took the uplands of the Middle Reach and the west: not wildfire, though it fathered wildfires, but a burning that fell and flowed, that took stone as readily as forest, that turned the sky the color of a dirty seal for three years of failed harvests. On the coasts it came differently and worse: the sea itself burned in patches, and where burning water met sand it left sheets and ropes of glass, and the tide brings glass ashore on those coasts to this hour.

Its cause carries more claimed authors than any event I have recorded, and I will honor my vow one last bitter time and resolve nothing: a Covenant deep-forge breached in the sealed mountains; a Thaumic great work, half-built through the whole late war by one power or several, loosed unfinished by the Failing of its restraints; the Drowned Star's partisans say the star, waking; the hearth-faiths say the lease, called in. I record what every account shares: it began in no country's heartland and spared no country's border, and no herald ever came forward to claim it, which in twenty-three centuries of recorded war had never once been true of any deliberate fire.

> The Grey Weir ledgers end in RR 2313 with an entry in my hand that I copy here entire, because I have never improved on it: 'No travelers. Ash on the water since the eighth day. The stone is quiet. Continuing.'

chronicle/viii-the-long-ash.body:
> An age is not dark because nothing happens. It is dark because no one is left whose business is to watch.

From the Ashfall to the first rekindled charters ran one hundred and thirty years and some — the span the hearthfolk call the Long Ash. It is the worst-attested age since the Unwritten World, for the plain reason that the watchers were dead, scattered, or, in one case, walking the ruined toll-roads with a pack of ledgers, writing down what remained. This chapter is thinner than those before it. I was one clerk, on foot, in a broken world. I got what I could.

## What the world became

- **The hearthlands.** The Failing's deepest wound was distance itself. With no stone to hold a stranger's word, the world's working size shrank to the range of a man's own reputation — a valley, a river-reach, a coast. The ruined waystations, squatting at every ford and pass, marked the borders of these shrunken worlds like headstones. Men settled *between* them, in the sheltered pockets, and the pockets grew inward. These are the hearthlands, and the reader lives in one.
- **The plague years.** Ash-lung rode the dirty sky through every land three harvests running, and returned each dry summer for a generation. The living learned again to burn their dead quickly, which — I record the fact without comment, and the reader who has followed me this far will hear the comment anyway — made the Grave-touched arts at once more feared and more employed than in any age before.
- **The road powers.** Between the hearthlands moved the age's true sovereigns: mercenary companies paid in grain and girls, salvage brotherhoods stripping the waystations of their lead and wax, ruin-cults who worshipped at the quiet stones, and the monster domains — I use the settled folk's word — of the high cold and the deep places, which spread into lands men had held for two thousand years and hold them yet. Maps of the age mark such country honestly: *theirs*.
- **The false rekindlings.** Four times in the Long Ash, to my own knowledge, someone raised a stone and claimed the Roads were returning. Three were frauds of the ordinary kind, selling attestation no lattice backed. The fourth — at Cold Ford itself, in RR 2389, led by a woman the crowds called the First Witness Come Again — I traveled four hundred miles to see. I sat before her stone three days and heard it attest nothing, and said so in writing, and her people broke my hands and burned my pack. Ledgers can be recopied; I had duplicates buried in three counties. Hands mend, in my condition, slowly. I include the entry because the reader should know the price of the vow this book is written under, and who has paid it.

## What endured

Not nothing. It is the clerk's duty to record the credits with the debits, and the Long Ash held credits. Seed-grain crossed the dry country in Synod caravans and was not poisoned. The Deepfen took in three waves of Reedfen refugees and drowned none of them, whatever the upstream ballads claim. In the burnt uplands, the families who would become the wardens of the Cinder March held the pass-forts against the road powers for four unpaid generations, because someone had held them in their grandmothers' time and no one had ordered them to stop. And in every hearthland, in every generation, without exception and without coordination, the folk kept two habits the Failing could not sever: they taught their children letters, and they swore their little bargains at the quiet stones anyway — *for the habit of the thing*, they said. I have come to believe — one more unclerkly sentence, and the last — that the habit of the thing is the load-bearing wall of the world, and that the Roads were only ever its monument.

> It was in these years the candles began appearing at my door, and the name Ledgerbone attached to me. A lich who pays for lodging in fair copies of lost title-deeds acquires, over a century, a reputation of a complicated kind. I have been stoned out of eleven towns and begged back into nine of them, always for the same reason: sooner or later, every hearthland needs to prove what its grandfathers actually owned.

chronicle/ix-the-rekindled-hearths.body:
> Keep the hearth. Keep the oath. — the whole of the Ashen Compact's founding charter that anyone bothers to quote; the rest is grain-schedules, and I have read the rest

In the last two generations the Long Ash has ended — not by proclamation but by symptom. Roads are being paved by subscription again. Charters are being sealed that strangers honor. Wayfinders are mapping past the ruined stations, and the maps *sell*. Four powers of the new kind now stand in the lands this book has walked, and I set them down as they stand in RR 2447, with their virtues, their quarrels, and their inheritances from everything recorded above. They are small, by the measure of [IV. The Age of Crowns](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/iv-the-age-of-crowns). So were the nineteen communities at Cold Ford.

## The Ashen Compact

**Banner: hearth-gold. Word: *Keep the hearth. Keep the oath.***  The Compact is what the displaced made of displacement: the craft households burned out of the old upland towns in the Ashfall, knitted together over four generations by public oaths sworn in open square — for they trust no sealed room, and having read this book the reader knows why. Its hearth councils prize the reliable workshop above all things; their cinder-masons' reusable kiln-forms are the quiet marvel of the age, and a Compact journeyman's mark on a tool is the nearest thing the hearthlands have to attested value. Their standing quarrel is grain: how much of the common store the frontier settlements may draw before they have proven out. It is argued in council, publicly, interminably, and — I record this with something a mortal writer would be permitted to call affection — *honestly*. They are the only power in this chapter that has never once asked me to alter a record. They ask me to witness them instead.

## The Reedbound Council

**Banner: reed-green. Word: *No river belongs to one shore.***  The wetland villages of the Reedfen margin, bound by seasonal assemblies as their fen-court landlords bound them in elder days — the form is pure Mire Courts, and the Council would sooner drown than admit it. Between assemblies the Council barely exists; in assembly season it is the shrewdest single body of bargainers in the hearthlands, for these are folk who survived the Failing's refugee years on their neighbors' terms and buried the memory shallow, where it works. Their standing quarrel is drainage: the upstream landholders cut channels and the downstream boat families lose the deep water they live by, and every assembly ends with the matter tabled, because the Council's true constitution is the shared knowledge that the fen outlasts everyone who tries to own it outright.

## The Cinder March

**Banner: burnt-rose. Word: *We hold what the fire spared.***  The pass-fort families of the burnt uplands, hardened by four unpaid generations into a hereditary wardenship, now paid at last — and there is the quarrel. The mines under the fells have reopened, and the miners' coin finances walls the wardens once held on habit alone, and men who finance a thing eventually ask why they do not direct it. Warden and mine-master need each other, resent the needing, and both arm accordingly. The March is the most fortified, most disciplined, and poorest of the four powers, and its shield-drill — formations trained to cover one another as the old Throne infantry never learned to — is studied by every captain in the hearthlands. If war comes to the rekindled lands, whichever side has the March holds the high country; every power in this chapter knows it; the March knows they know. That is a whole politics, and I have set it down in one sentence, and the reader may have the sentence free.

## The Glass Tide

**Banner: sea-grey. Word: *Every horizon is a promise.***  The charter towns of the vitrified coast, who took their name from the Ashfall's glass and their habits from the drowned League — charters, shares, pledged keels, the whole grammar of the old paper sea, rebuilt small and cautious by folk who pick their ancestors' catastrophe off the beach every morning. The Tide's standing quarrel is its own founding question: the old routes past the coast are dangerous — glass-shoals, road powers, and worse things attested farther out — and reopening each one is a public work that every town wants opened and no town wants to fund. Their assemblies are auctions of blame. And yet the routes *do* reopen, one by one, because the Tide holds the League's true inheritance, which was never the fleets: it is the conviction, bred deeper than grief, that the horizon is owed to them.

---

> Beyond the four: the mountains hold and do not answer; the terraces endure and do not explain; the Deepfen watches its former tenants prosper with whatever the fen-courts use for feelings; the road powers still rule the wide ruin between the hearthlands; and the monster domains have had a hundred and thirty years of unwatched increase. The rekindled lands are a clearing in a very old forest. I say so not to darken the reader's hope but to size it honestly, which is what hope is for.

chronicle/x-the-present-hour.body:
> Maps and promises have become valuable again. Everything in this book is the price history charged to make that sentence possible.

It is the year 2447 of a reckoning only I still keep. I write this final chapter in the tower at Grey Weir, above a ford where wagons cross again after a century of silence, and I record the present hour as I have recorded every hour: as evidence, for those who come after. This is the world as it stands — the world in which the reader now acts.

## The shape of the hour

- **Hearth caravans** go out each spring past the edge of the drawn maps, whole households under canvas, to found what their charters gravely call settlements and their mothers call graves-in-waiting. Some prove out. More every year.
- **Wayfinders** — the new age's scouts, half surveyor and half burglar — sell what the Roads once gave: knowledge of what lies past the next ruined station. Their maps are copied, forged, stolen, and killed over. I have authenticated maps for three parties to the same murder, and the reader now knows everything worth knowing about the map trade.
- **Oath guards** stand at the new markets and the sworn boundaries, and the title is exact, and no one who uses it knows why it makes me stand still a moment. They guard oaths. It is a beginning.
- **Public ledgers** — 'civic accounts,' the Compact's clerks call them — spread from market to market, open books in open squares, reconnecting bargain to bargain the slow way, by daylight and audit, as the stones once did in the dark for free. It is slower. It may — one entry of judgment, at the end of the book, as an old clerk's fee — it may be sounder.
- **The fourteen springs** run on, indifferent to the ages; the hedge-teachers are becoming schools again, the schools will become colleges, and colleges, as this book has shown at length, become estates of power. The traditions and disciplines the new mages will fight over are set out in the [Appendix — The Fourteen Traditions](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/appendix-the-fourteen-traditions). Nothing in that appendix has changed since the Unwritten World. Everything else has, twice.

## What the hour will become

I am asked to prophesy, in the towns that beg me back. I refuse; prophecy is motive-writing about the future. But a clerk may extrapolate, and I will close the book with the extrapolation I give the councils that ask honestly. The rekindled powers are entering an age of fracture — small worlds, jealous borders, everything to found and everything to lose. If it runs as the last cycle ran, fracture will breed crowns, and crowns will breed a reckoning, and some clerk not yet born will write the whole bill out again under a colder title. **It is not required to run as the last cycle ran.** That is the entire yield of twenty-three centuries of records, and I set it down as the finding of this book: the Failing was not fate but bookkeeping, entry by entry, each one chosen, each one attested, each one refusable at the time by the people who did not refuse it.

Five roads out of the fracture are visible already from my tower, and I name them as a wayfinder names passes, without blessing any: dominion, by which the strong make the quarrels stop; hegemony, by which the cunning make the quarrels theirs; prosperity, by which the diligent make the quarrels unaffordable; legacy, by which the patient outlast them; and ascendancy, by which someone — there is always someone; see [VI. The Reckoning](/theandril/atlas/chronicle/vi-the-reckoning) — reaches past the fourteen springs for the machinery underneath. Against that last road this book is my only levy, and I have made it as heavy as I could.

---

Here my record ends, not because the story ends but because the present is not the chronicler's country. What happens next belongs to the living: to the councils and the marches, the caravans and the wayfinders, the grain-quarrels and the drainage-quarrels and the quiet stones watching the new banners pass. Act, then, knowing what it cost to win back a world where promises can be kept — and when your own age closes, whatever it has made of itself, see that somebody honest writes it down. There will be another book. Let it be a **book of rekindled hearths**, and let it be true, and if its writer needs the old ledgers, the tower at Grey Weir keeps a light. It is only a candle at the door. I told you the custom was useless. I never said it was unwelcome.

> Sealed at Grey Weir, RR 2447, by Ilthen Vael, Third Recorder, struck from the rolls — the record continuing.

chronicle/appendix-the-fourteen-traditio.body:
> Magic is not a thing men have. It is a thing places and bloodlines and bargains leak. — hedge-teaching, all ages

For readers of the coming age who will meet these powers on the field, at the council table, or in their own children: the springs of magic as twenty-three centuries of records attest them. A tradition is an *inheritance* — an aptitude carried in blood, place, or pact, determining what a given soul can wield. A discipline is a *knowledge* — what a realm's scholars have worked out about wielding it. The two are forever confused by the ignorant and forever separated in practice: a realm may hold deep theory no living subject can perform, and a marsh-child may carry aptitude no school has words for. Every catastrophe in this book except the honest ones began in the gap between those two.

## The fourteen springs

- **Flame** — destruction, heat, the forge, purification. The Kiln faith's darling; the Ashfall's suspect.
- **Storm** — lightning, wind, weather, the high air. League pilots married into it for generations, deliberately.
- **Tide** — water, cold, navigation, the sea's consent. The Glass Tide's coasts are thick with the aptitude and poor, so far, in its schooling.
- **Stone** — earth, endurance, fortification, metal in the ground. The Anvilheights' other treasury.
- **Verdancy** — growth, beasts, healing, the wild. The Deepfen's first estate; distrusted by every besieger who has watched a wall hedge itself overnight.
- **Grave** — death, the housed dead, decay and its arrest. My own condition's spring. Feared everywhere, employed everywhere, honest about neither.
- **Star** — divination, distance, portals, fate's paperwork. The Synod's far-writing and the League's navigation both drew here; so, some claim, did the Roads.
- **Dream** — illusion, sleep, morale, the inward country. The Covenant bred it out and boasted; the reader has seen what a folk that cannot lie to itself did anyway.
- **Shadow** — concealment, curses, the unwatched act. Every crown in this book kept Shadow servants and no crown ever admitted it in a treaty I sealed.
- **Radiance** — wards, revelation, the sacred fire. The exorcists' spring; the Hollowing made its practitioners wealthy and haunted in equal measure.
- **Spirit** — ancestors, possession, pact and shamanry. The old hearth religion entire; the Roads' folk-doctrine lives here.
- **Rune** — binding, inscription, artifice, the made thing that works. The Covenant's glory; the null-anchors' spring, which the reader should sit with.
- **Oath** — bond, lineage, sacrifice, the coercive sanctities. The spring of the stones themselves, by my order's doctrine; the spring of soul-collateral, by demonstrated fact. Handle accordingly.
- **Void** — the outside power. I record of it only this: every age's records mention it, no age's records explain it, and the gaps in several archives I have copied are themselves the testimony. Where the reader finds a burned page in this world, read the burning.

## The nine disciplines

The old schools organized their knowledge nine ways, and the new schools are already rediscovering the same shelves: **Calling**, which summons and binds; **Transmutation**, which changes body, matter, and land; **Projection**, which makes the springs into weapons at distance; **Warding**, which shields, dispels, and nullifies — the Throne's whole genius; **Artifice**, which fixes power into things; **Veilcraft**, which deceives — the counterfeit seals were Veilcraft, and the reader has seen the invoice; **Malison**, which curses and afflicts; **Thaumic Dominion**, which works at the scale of weather, realm, and age, and stands accused by half my sources of the Ashfall itself; and the **Forbidden Arts**, which are forbidden, and which every power in this book kept a locked drawer of anyway, and which made the hand that writes this sentence. The reader will find no hypocrisy in me on the last point. Only the record, and the request that the coming age read it before opening the drawer.

> A last note for the practical. Aptitude without knowledge is a child with a coal. Knowledge without aptitude is a library in a language no one speaks. Realms rise on the match between the two — and fall, this book attests from end to end, on the mismatch. Count your casters before you covet your neighbor's theory. — I.V.
